Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 44, verses 47–48:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾ (47) ﴿Then pour over his head the torment of boiling water.﴾ (48)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: ﴿Seize him﴾, meaning this sinful one who disbelieved in his Lord, of whom God, whose praise is exalted, has informed that the tree of zaqqum is his food. ﴿Then drag him﴾: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: push him and drive him forward. It is said of this: ʿatalahu, yaʿtiluhu, ʿatlan, when one drives him with pushing and pulling. From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Noble men are not those who withhold their fathers [from being given] until ʿAṭiyya is reached and dragged along (tuʿtal).[[The verse is in the Diwan of al-Farazdaq (Sawi edition, Cairo, p. 722), and "nahilika" means "your giver." The point of evidence in the verse is his saying "tuʿtal." It is said in (Lisan al-ʿArab, ʿ-t-l): In the revelation, "Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire." ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Abu ʿAmr read "fa-ʿtiluhu" with a kasra on the tāʾ; Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Yaʿqūb read "fa-ʿtulūhu" with a ḍamma on the tāʾ. Al-Azharī said: both are eloquent dialects. Its meaning: seize him and break him as wood is broken. Al-ʿAtl means pushing and driving with violent force. End of quotation.]]

That is, he is driven forward, pushed and dragged.

Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and his companions whom Allah, blessed and exalted, killed on the day of Badr: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for disbelief and caused their people to alight at the abode of destruction?﴾

Qatadah said: Abu Jahl said: "Between its two mountains there is no man mightier or more noble than I," so Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Taste! Indeed you were the mighty, the noble.﴾

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Hellfire﴾: "This is for Abu Jahl."

If someone says: How is it said, while he is being humiliated by the punishment Allah mentioned, and being dragged into the midst of the Hellfire in disgrace: "Indeed you were the mighty, the noble"? It is said: His words ﴿Indeed you were the mighty, the noble﴾ are not a description by the one saying this of him as mighty and noble, but rather a rebuke from Him to him with what he used to describe himself with in the world, and a reproach to him in that manner, by way of quoting. For he used to say in the world: "Indeed I am the mighty, the noble." So it is said to him in the Hereafter, when he is punished with what he is punished with in the Fire: "Taste this humiliation today, for you used to claim that you were the mighty, the noble, and that you were [in truth] the abased and the contemptible. Where is that which you used to say and claim of might and nobility? Why did you not restrain the punishment by your might?"

* Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Safwan ibn Isa narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ajlan narrated to us, from Sa'id al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: Ka'b said: "Allah has three garments: He wraps Himself in might (izzar), clothes Himself in mercy (tasarbul), and dons greatness (ridaʾ al-kibriyaʾ), exalted is His mention. Whoever claims might by other than what Allah has made mighty, that is the one to whom it is said: ﴿Taste! Indeed you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ Whoever shows mercy to people, that is the one whom Allah clothes in the garment that befits him. Whoever is arrogant, that is the one who contends with Allah for His cloak. Indeed Allah, exalted is His mention, says: 'Whoever contends with Me for My cloak, I will not admit him into Paradise,' mighty and majestic is He."

The readers of the cities all agreed on the kasra of the alif in ﴿Taste! Indeed (inna) you﴾, as a new sentence and a quotation of the speech of this speaker: "Indeed I am the mighty, the noble." Some later readers read ﴿Taste that (anna) you﴾ with a fatha on the alif, governing ﴿Taste﴾ over ﴿anna you﴾, as if the meaning of the speech in their view were: "Taste this statement which you made in the world."

The correct reading in this matter, in our view, is the kasra of the alif in ﴿inna﴾, according to the meaning I have mentioned to its reader, because of the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it, and the anomaly of what opposes it. [[His words "and the anomaly of what opposes it": this is incorrect, because Imam al-Kisa'i read with the fatha of the hamza, and it is a canonical, mutawatir, well-known reading and not anomalous.]] And the practice of the earlier and later Imams in following it is sufficient proof of the error of reading otherwise, along with its distance from correctness in meaning and its departure from the interpretation of the people of interpretation.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 44, verse 51–53:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place, among gardens and springs, wearing [garments of] fine silk and brocade, facing one another.﴾

His saying, exalted is He, means: Indeed, those who fear Allah by performing His obedience and avoiding His disobediences will be in a place of abiding, secure in that place from what they used to fear in the abodes of this world: illnesses, ailments, idols, and griefs.

The reciters differed in reading His saying ﴿fī maqāmin amīn﴾ (in a secure place). The majority of the reciters of Medina read it ﴿fī muqāmin amīn﴾ with a dammah on the mīm, meaning: in a secure place of abiding (iqāmah) free from departure (ẓa'n). The majority of the reciters of the two garrison cities, Kufa and Basra, read ﴿fī maqāmin﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm, according to the meaning we have described, directing it to mean that they are in a secure place and location.

The correct view regarding this is that both are widely transmitted readings among the readers of the metropolitan cities, and both are sound in meaning; whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

Ahl al-ta'wil (the exegetes) said things in agreement with what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place﴾: "Yes, by Allah, secure from Satan, idols, and griefs."

And His saying ﴿among gardens and springs﴾

The gardens and springs are an explanation of the secure place; the secure place is the gardens and springs. The gardens (jannat) are orchards, and the springs (ʿuyūn) are springs of water flowing at the roots of the trees of the gardens.

And His saying ﴿wearing [garments of] fine silk﴾

He says: these righteous ones will wear, in these gardens, sundus, which is the thinner part of brocade (dībāj), and istabraq, which is the thicker part of brocade.

As related:

Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Ikrimah, regarding His saying ﴿of sundus and istabraq﴾, he said: Istabraq is thick brocade.

It was said: ﴿yalbasūna min sundusin wa istabraq﴾ without saying "libāsan," relying on the meaning of the statement to indicate it.

And His saying ﴿facing one another﴾

It means that in Paradise they will face one another with their faces, and none of them will look at the back of another.

We have already mentioned the narrations on this earlier, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 44, verses 54–57:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Thus. And We will marry them to fair-skinned women with large, beautiful eyes. They will call therein for every fruit, secure. They will not taste therein death, except the first death. And He will protect them from the punishment of Hellfire. As a bounty from your Lord. That is the great attainment.﴾

Says God, may He be remembered: Just as We gave these pious ones in the Hereafter honor by admitting them into the Gardens, and clothing them therein with green silk and brocade, so We have also honored them by marrying them, therein, to ḥūr (ḥūr, the plural of ḥawrā’, "women with pure whiteness") from among the women, and they are the pure in whiteness; the singular of them is ḥawrā’.

Mujahid used to say concerning the meaning of ḥūr, that:

Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa’ narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿and We will marry them to ḥūr ‘īn﴾: he said, "We wed them to ḥūr." He said: The ḥūr are those whose gaze is dazzled by them, the marrow of whose shins is visible through their garments, and the beholder can see his face in the liver of one of them like a mirror, from the thinness of the skin and the clearness of the complexion. And this which Mujahid said, that the meaning of ḥūr is only that the gaze is dazzled by them, is a statement that has no meaning in the speech of the Arabs, because ḥūr is only the plural of ḥawrā’, like ḥumr, the plural of ḥamrā’, and sūd, the plural of sawdā’; and ḥawrā’ is from the pattern fa‘lā’ of ḥaṣr, which is the purity of whiteness, just as the purest white flour is called ḥuwwārī. We have already explained the meaning of this, with its evidence, earlier.

And in the same manner as what we have said regarding this meaning, all the people of interpretation have said.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa‘id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Thus, and We will marry them to ḥūr ‘īn﴾: he said, "white, large-eyed." He said: And in the recitation of Ibn Mas‘ud, ﴿bi‘īsin ‘īn﴾.

Ibn ‘Abd al-A‘la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma‘mar, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿bi-ḥūrin ‘īn﴾ he said: "white, ‘īn." He said: And in the reading of Ibn Mas‘ud, ﴿bi‘īsin ‘īn﴾. Ibn Mas‘ud recited this, meaning that the meaning of ḥūr is other than what Mujahid held, because ‘īs among the Arabs is the plural of ‘ays’ā’, which is the white-coloured she-camel, as al-A‘sha said:

"And a wilderness distant, its paths empty, wolves howl over it; I burdened a white camel beneath the saddle, swift in its pace."

Here "a‘ays" means a white camel. As for ‘īn, it is the plural of ‘ayna’, which is a woman with large eyes.

* *

As for His words ﴿They will call therein﴾ … the verse. It means: these pious ones will call in the Garden for every kind of fruit of the Garden that they desire, secure therein from its cessation, its exhaustion and its end, and from the harm of its injury and its unpleasantness. That is to say: that fruit there is not like the fruit of this world that we eat, about which they would fear the harm of its consequence, the aftermath of its injury, along with its exhaustion from them and its absence at some times and seasons.

Qatadah used to direct the interpretation of His words ﴿secure﴾ toward what:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa‘id narrated to us, from Qatadah, ﴿They will call therein for every fruit, secure﴾: "They are secure from death, from ailments, and from Satan."

* *

As for His words ﴿They will not taste therein death, except the first death﴾

God, may He be remembered, says: These pious ones in the Garden will not taste death after the first death which they tasted in this world.

Some of the grammarians of Arabic held that "illā" (except) in this place is in the sense of "siwā" (other than), and said: the meaning of the speech is: they will not taste therein death other than the first death, and he gave as an example His words, may He be remembered: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾, meaning: other than what your fathers did. But there is no intelligible sense to what he said in my view, because the most common usage of the speaker who says "I will not taste food today except the food I tasted before today" is that he intends to inform that he has food on that day which he tastes and eats, other than all other foods.

Since that is the most common of its meaning, it would be necessary that by His words ﴿except the first death﴾ a death of the kind of the first be affirmed which they taste; and it is known that this is not so, because God, mighty and majestic, has granted the people of the Garden security from death once they have entered it. Rather, it is as I have described its meaning. It is permissible for "illā" to be placed in the position of "ba‘da" (after) because their meanings converge in this place: for whoever says, "I will not speak today to any man except a man after a man at ‘Amr's," has committed himself not to speak that day to any man after the speech of the man at ‘Amr's.

Likewise, if he says, "I will not speak today to any man after a man at ‘Amr's," he has committed himself not to speak that day to any man except a man at ‘Amr's, so "ba‘da" and "illā" are close in meaning in this place. It is the habit of the Arabs to place a word in the position of another when their meanings converge, as when they place "rajā’" (hope) in the position of "khawf" (fear), because there is fear in the meaning of hope, since hope is not certainty but longing, and it may be true or false, just as fear may sometimes be true and sometimes false. Abu Dhu’ayb said in that:

"When the wasp stings him, he does not hope for its sting, and it opposed him in a house of cloud-cover, bees…"

He said: "lam yarju las‘ahā" (he did not hope for its sting), meaning: he did not fear its sting. And like their placing "ẓann" (supposition) in the position of "‘ilm" (knowledge) which was not gained by sight, but was gained by inference or report, as the poet said:

"I said to them, 'Suppose [ẓannū] two thousand armoured men, their leaders in the sharpened Persian mail.'"

Meaning: be certain of two thousand armoured men and know. So "ẓann" was placed in the position of certainty, since those addressed had not seen the two thousand armoured men nor beheld them, and only this informant told them of it; so he said to them "ẓannū," meaning knowledge of what was not seen, an act of the heart, and so one was placed in the position of the other because their meanings converge, in many similar cases which are too numerous to count, just as two words converge in meaning in some respects while differing in others, and the Arabs place one of them in the position of its companion where their meanings converge.

Likewise His words ﴿They will not taste therein death, except the first death﴾: "illā" was placed in the position of "ba‘da" because of the convergence of the meaning of "illā" and "ba‘da" in this place. Likewise ﴿and do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ means: after what has passed among you in the Jahiliyyah. As for interpreting "illā" in this place as "siwā" (other than), that is merely a translation from the place and an explanation of it by something more ambiguous for one who wishes to know its meaning.

* *

As for His words ﴿And He will protect them from the punishment of Hellfire, as a bounty from your Lord﴾

God, may He be remembered, says: And He protected these pious ones from the punishment of the Fire on that Day, as a bounty from you, O Muhammad, from your Lord upon them, and as a kindness from Him to them thereby, and He did not punish them for a sin they committed in the world. Had it not been for His bounty upon them in pardoning them from the punishment for what they had committed of that in the world, He would not have protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire, but its pain and harm would have reached and afflicted them.

* *

As for His words ﴿That is the great attainment﴾

God, may He be remembered, says: This which We have given these pious ones in the Hereafter of the honor described in these verses is the great attainment; that is: it is the great victory, with what they used to seek to attain in this world by their deeds, their obedience to their Lord, and their piety toward Him in what He tested them with of obedience and obligations, and their avoidance of what is forbidden.

We have already explained the meaning of this, with its evidence, earlier.

And in the same manner as what we have said regarding this meaning, all the people of interpretation have said.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 44, verses 58–59:

On the interpretation of His saying, ﴿So We have made it easy in your tongue, that they may remember (58). So wait, [O Muhammad], for they are waiting (59).﴾

His saying, exalted is His remembrance, to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Indeed, We have made easy the recitation of this Qur'an which We have revealed to you, O Muhammad, in your tongue, so that these polytheists, to whom We sent you, may remember through its admonitions and proofs, be warned by its exhortations, and reflect upon its signs when you recite it to them; then they may turn in repentance to the obedience of their Lord, and submit to the truth once they have clarified it for themselves.

As narrated:

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿So We have made it easy in your tongue﴾: That is, this Qur'an, ﴿that they may remember﴾.

* Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿So We have made it easy in your tongue﴾: He said: The Qur'an. And "made it easy" means: He loosened his tongue with it.

* * *

And as for His saying ﴿So wait, [O Muhammad], for they are waiting﴾:

His saying, exalted is His remembrance, to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: So await, O Muhammad, the victory from your Lord and the triumph over these polytheists among your people from Quraysh, who in their own minds await your subjugation and defeat, by barring people from the truth you have brought to those who wish to accept it and follow you in it.

The exegetes have said what is similar to what we have said regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿So wait, for they are waiting﴾.

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿So wait, for they are waiting﴾: That is, wait, for they are waiting.
